stem: A root dbt project defines its own custom macro for generating a model's schema name. Two installed packages, unrelated to each other, each also happen to define a macro with that exact same name. A developer needs to know which of these three definitions dbt actually uses when it builds a model. Which one wins, and why?

option_texts.A: The root project's own macro wins, because dbt always ignores a same-named macro coming from any package
option_texts.B: Whichever package happens to be listed first in `packages.yml` wins over the project's own macro
option_texts.C: dbt raises a compilation error, since three separate definitions of the same macro name is ambiguous
option_texts.D: dbt merges the logic from all three definitions into a single combined macro at parse time

drill_answer_short: A project's own generate_schema_name macro wins; dbt ignores any package-defined versions
decision_hinge: If your dbt project has a custom macro called generate_schema_name, dbt will use it instead of the default macro. Be careful: dbt will ignore any custom generate_schema_name macros included in installed packages.

B.signal: Two installed packages, unrelated to each other, each also happen to define a macro with that exact same name
B.requires_fact: dbt will ignore any custom generate_schema_name macros included in installed packages, regardless of install order.

eliminated_by.C: A developer needs to know which of these three definitions dbt actually uses when it builds a model
eliminated_by.D: A developer needs to know which of these three definitions dbt actually uses when it builds a model

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — a package-defined version of this macro is ignored entirely, regardless of install order
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — dbt resolves this deterministically in favor of the project's own macro, it does not error
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt does not merge multiple macro definitions together

stem: A `dbt_project.yml` sets `models: airbnb: +grants: {select: ["transform", "reporter"]} +post-hook: ["INSERT INTO {{ target.schema }}.audit_log VALUES (...)"]`. The team needs to know what each of these two configs actually controls once a model in `airbnb` finishes building. What does each one do?

option_texts.A: `+grants` ensures the model's view or table grants match the configured privileges; `+post-hook` runs the given SQL statement right after the model is built
option_texts.B: `+grants` runs SQL after the build finishes; `+post-hook` ensures permissions match the configured privileges
option_texts.C: Both configs do the same thing: they run arbitrary SQL statements after the model builds
option_texts.D: `+grants` and `+post-hook` only apply to seeds and snapshots, never to models

drill_answer_short: grants reconciles permissions to match config; post-hook runs SQL right after the model builds
decision_hinge: When your model finishes building, dbt ensures that the grants on its view or table match exactly the grants you have configured. post-hook is executed after a model, seed or snapshot is built.

plausible_options.C: once a model in `airbnb` finishes building

eliminated_by.B: once a model in `airbnb` finishes building
eliminated_by.D: once a model in `airbnb` finishes building

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the two configs' roles are swapped here; grants reconciles permissions, post-hook runs SQL
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — grants reconciles permissions to match config; running arbitrary SQL is what hooks are for
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — both grants and hooks apply to models, seeds, and snapshots alike

stem: A column description in `schema.yml` uses `description: '{{ doc("dim_listing_cleansed__minimum_nights") }}'` instead of a plain markdown string. The team needs to know what this `{{ doc() }}` reference actually does when the docs site is generated. What does it do?

option_texts.A: It expands to the text content defined in a separate `{% docs %}` block with that same name
option_texts.B: It runs a SQL query against the model to generate a live description from the data itself
option_texts.C: It inserts the column's data type automatically, inferred from the model's compiled SQL
option_texts.D: It creates a new docs block with that name if one doesn't already exist

drill_answer_short: doc() expands to the markdown content of a matching {% docs %} block
decision_hinge: To use a docs block, reference it from your schema.yml file with the doc() function in place of a markdown string. In the resulting documentation, the doc() reference will be expanded to the markdown defined in that docs block.

plausible_options.C: instead of a plain markdown string

eliminated_by.B: The team needs to know what this `{{ doc() }}` reference actually does when the docs site is generated
eliminated_by.D: The team needs to know what this `{{ doc() }}` reference actually does when the docs site is generated

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — doc() expands a static markdown block, it does not query the model's data
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — doc() expands markdown text, it has no connection to inferring a data type from compiled SQL
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — doc() references an existing block; it does not create one automatically

stem: A team sets `persist_docs: {relation: true, columns: true}` on an ephemeral model, hoping its column descriptions will appear as warehouse comments. The team needs to know whether this actually works, given what `persist_docs` writes and what an ephemeral model creates. What happens?

option_texts.A: Nothing is written anywhere, because an ephemeral model produces no database object for `persist_docs` to attach comments to
option_texts.B: The comments are written onto the CTE this ephemeral model compiles into inside its downstream models
option_texts.C: `persist_docs` silently converts the model to a view so it has something to comment on
option_texts.D: The comments are written to the generated docs site HTML instead of the warehouse

drill_answer_short: persist_docs writes comments on database objects; an ephemeral model creates none to write to
decision_hinge: persist_docs optionally persists resource descriptions as column and relation comments in the database. An ephemeral model is not built directly into the database; dbt interpolates its code into dependent models as a CTE.

plausible_options.C: hoping its column descriptions will appear as warehouse comments

eliminated_by.B: hoping its column descriptions will appear as warehouse comments
eliminated_by.D: given what `persist_docs` writes and what an ephemeral model creates

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — persist_docs comments attach to a database object, not to an interpolated CTE fragment
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — persist_docs has no documented ability to override a model's own configured materialization
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — persist_docs is explicitly about database comments, a separate mechanism from the generated docs site itself

stem: A team wants to add a Markdown-formatted description to a model that is too long for inline YAML, so they write a doc block in a `.md` file. Complete the opening tag syntax for a docs block named `dim_listing_cleansed__minimum_nights`: ____ dim_listing_cleansed__minimum_nights %}
drill_answer_short: A docs block opens with {% docs <name> %} and closes with {% enddocs %}
decision_hinge: {% docs table_events %} This table contains clickstream events from the marketing website. ... {% enddocs %}

stem: A team drafts an exposure with `name: executive_dashboard`, `label: Executive Dashboard`, `type: dashboard`, `maturity: low`, and a `url`, but no `owner` property anywhere. The reviewer needs to know which TWO statements about this draft are correct, before approving it.

option_texts.A: `name` and `type` are both required, and both are present and valid here
option_texts.B: The exposure is invalid as drafted, because `owner` is a required property and it is missing entirely
option_texts.C: `maturity` is a required property too, so this exposure would be invalid even if `owner` were added
option_texts.D: `url` is a required property too, so this exposure would be invalid even if `owner` were added

drill_answer_short: name and type are required and present; owner is also required but missing here
decision_hinge: Required: name, a unique exposure name written in snake case; type, one of dashboard, notebook, analysis, ml, application; owner, name or email required.

plausible_options.C: A team drafts an exposure with `name: executive_dashboard`, `label: Executive Dashboard`, `type: dashboard`, `maturity: low`, and a `url`, but no `owner` property anywhere

eliminated_by.D: A team drafts an exposure with `name: executive_dashboard`, `label: Executive Dashboard`, `type: dashboard`, `maturity: low`, and a `url`, but no `owner` property anywhere

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — maturity is optional documentation metadata, not a required property
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — url is optional context for consumers, not a mandatory field

stem: A release engineer runs `dbt build --select +exposure:executive_dashboard`. The exposure depends on two models, which each have their own upstream chains feeding into them. The team needs to know exactly which resources this command builds. What gets built?

option_texts.A: Every model upstream of the exposure, following both dependency chains back to their sources, plus the exposure's two direct parents
option_texts.B: Only the exposure's two direct parent models, since `exposure:` selectors do not traverse further upstream
option_texts.C: Every model in the entire project, since an exposure feeding off two upstream chains could in principle depend on anything
option_texts.D: Nothing is built; exposure selectors only work with `dbt test` and `dbt ls`, never `dbt build`

drill_answer_short: A leading + on an exposure selector traverses its full upstream lineage, not just its direct parents
decision_hinge: dbt run --select +exposure:weekly_kpis runs all models that feed into the weekly_kpis exposure. Placed before a model/resource, the + operator includes the resource itself and all its ancestors.

plausible_options.B: which each have their own upstream chains feeding into them

eliminated_by.C: The team needs to know exactly which resources this command builds
eliminated_by.D: The team needs to know exactly which resources this command builds

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the leading + traverses the full upstream lineage, not just the direct parents
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — the + operator scopes to the exposure's own lineage, not the whole project
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — exposure selectors work with dbt build the same as other selection methods

stem: A `packages.yml` lists `dbt-labs/dbt_utils` and `calogica/dbt_expectations`. The team needs to know exactly what makes the macros from both packages available for use in project models, since just editing `packages.yml` alone does not seem to be enough. What's the missing step, and why?

option_texts.A: Running `dbt deps`; package macros only become available once dbt has actually pulled each listed dependency into the project
option_texts.B: Nothing else is needed; editing `packages.yml` makes every listed package's macros available immediately
option_texts.C: Restarting the warehouse connection, since package macros are registered at the database level, not the project level
option_texts.D: Manually copying each package's macro files into the project's own `macros/` folder

drill_answer_short: dbt deps must run to actually pull listed packages before their macros are available
decision_hinge: dbt deps pulls the most recent version of the dependencies listed in your packages.yml from git. Run dbt deps to install the package(s).

plausible_options.C: since just editing `packages.yml` alone does not seem to be enough

eliminated_by.B: since just editing `packages.yml` alone does not seem to be enough
eliminated_by.D: since just editing `packages.yml` alone does not seem to be enough

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — editing packages.yml alone is exactly what the stem says is insufficient
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — package macro availability has nothing to do with the warehouse connection itself
distractor_traps.D: T7: over-engineering — dbt deps already pulls the package in; manually copying files duplicates that mechanism

stem: A snapshot is configured as YAML with a `relation:` property pointing at a raw table via `source()`, plus `config: {unique_key: id, strategy: timestamp, updated_at: updated_at}`. The team needs to know exactly what `relation` points at here, and whether a `source()` call is valid syntax for it. What's true?

option_texts.A: `relation` names the input this snapshot reads from, and both `source(...)` and `ref(...)` are valid values for it
option_texts.B: `relation` is a deprecated alias for `target_schema`, which must be replaced before this config will parse
option_texts.C: `relation` only accepts a bare table name string, never a `source()` or `ref()` call
option_texts.D: `relation` configures where the snapshot's own output table is written, not what it reads from

drill_answer_short: relation names the source or model the snapshot reads from, accepting source() or ref()
decision_hinge: relation: relation # source('my_source', 'my_table') or ref('my_model'). This is how to reference the ephemeral model or source in the relation field.

plausible_options.C: exactly what `relation` points at here, and whether a `source()` call is valid syntax for it

eliminated_by.B: exactly what `relation` points at here, and whether a `source()` call is valid syntax for it
eliminated_by.D: exactly what `relation` points at here, and whether a `source()` call is valid syntax for it

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — relation is a current, documented YAML snapshot property, not a deprecated target_schema alias
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — some older config styles only took a bare table name; the current relation property accepts source() or ref()
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — relation names the input being snapshotted; the output table's location is controlled by separate schema/database config
